titre: Champollion and the Decipherment of Hieroglyphs (1822)
accroche: On September 14, 1822, Champollion rushes to his brother's, cries out “I've got it!”, and collapses for five days.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 14, 1822, Jean-François Champollion rushes into his elder brother's study in Paris and cries out: “I've got it!” In an instant, he has grasped the principle that makes it possible to read Egyptian hieroglyphs, a writing system that had stayed silent for more than 1,400 years. According to the family account, the emotion overwhelms him: he sinks into a kind of stupor from which, it is said, he does not rise until five days later.

## A Decree Carved Three Times on the Same Stone

The key lies in the Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799 near the Egyptian town of the same name: a decree issued in 196 BCE in honor of the pharaoh Ptolemy V, inscribed three times, in hieroglyphs, in Demotic script, and in ancient Greek. The Greek text, readable directly, makes it possible to guess the general meaning of the other two columns, but not to crack their mechanism: for two decades, European scholars and their rivals merely spot isolated correspondences, without understanding how the system works.

Champollion, who has mastered Coptic (the liturgical language of Egypt, descended directly from the language of the pharaohs), turns to the cartouches, those royal names ringed by an oval line. On a cartouche from a temple at Abu Simbel, he identifies the sun disk of the god Ra, then the signs corresponding to M and a doubled S: Ra-M-SS, that is, Ramesses. The same reasoning, applied to another cartouche, yields Thoth-M-S, Thutmose. The proof is there: Egyptian writing is not purely symbolic, as people had thought, nor purely phonetic; it combines the two, signs that record a sound and signs that record an idea. The English physicist Thomas Young, who had been working on the same problem for years, had already suspected that a cartouche could transcribe a sound; he had not gone so far as to accept this for properly Egyptian names, convinced that only foreign names were written that way.

## A Letter Read Before a Packed Hall

Thirteen days later, on September 27, 1822, Champollion presents his method to the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, in a letter addressed to its permanent secretary, Bon-Joseph Dacier: the *Lettre à M. Dacier relative à l'alphabet des hiéroglyphes phonétiques* (Letter to M. Dacier Concerning the Alphabet of Phonetic Hieroglyphs). The hall is packed, the demonstration causes a sensation, and the full text appears at the end of October from Firmin-Didot. Champollion immediately tests his alphabet on other monuments, including the base of an obelisk brought to England, and begins reading inscriptions that had been silent for fourteen centuries. The shift owes less to the anecdote of the cry and the fainting spell than to what it made possible: a script judged impenetrable because it was believed to be entirely symbolic turned out to follow a mixed system, which one only had to know how to look for.

citation.source: Words reported by his nephew Aimé-Louis Champollion-Figeac, September 14, 1822

carte.idee: On September 14, 1822, Champollion figures out how to read Egyptian hieroglyphs, silent for fourteen centuries. Thirteen days later, he presents his method to the Academy of Inscriptions: Egyptian writing mixes signs that record a sound with signs that record an idea.

quiz.question: How does the English physicist Thomas Young fail where Champollion succeeds?
choix: He refuses to accept that properly Egyptian names could be written phonetically
He does not have the Rosetta Stone to compare the three scripts
He is unaware of the existence of the cartouches enclosing royal names
He works alone, without the support of any learned academy
quiz.explication: Young had noticed that cartouches of foreign rulers, such as Ptolemy, recorded sounds, but remained convinced that native Egyptian names were written only symbolically: Champollion refuted this with Ramesses and Thutmose. It had nothing to do with the Rosetta Stone, the cartouches, or working alone.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799?
choix: An obelisk brought back from Egypt and checked by Champollion after he discovered the system
A decree from 196 BCE inscribed in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic, and ancient Greek
A Coptic manuscript found in a temple at Abu Simbel along with royal names
The original text of Champollion's treatise on the hieroglyphic alphabet
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The decree in honor of Ptolemy V is carved three times on the same stone, in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and ancient Greek, which makes it possible to compare the columns.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What allows Champollion to begin deciphering the royal cartouches?
choix: A hieroglyph-French dictionary compiled by Thomas Young a few years earlier
A Latin translation of the Demotic column made by a Coptic monk from Cairo
His mastery of Coptic, the liturgical language of Egypt, descended directly from the language of the pharaohs
The use of a new phonetic alphabet invented from scratch for the occasion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Champollion knew Coptic, the liturgical language of Egypt descended from that of the pharaohs, which allowed him to recognize the sounds recorded by the royal cartouches.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens on September 27, 1822, thirteen days after Champollion's cry?
choix: He publishes his complete alphabet with Firmin-Didot, before even testing it on other monuments
He leaves for Egypt to test his alphabet directly on the inscriptions of the temple at Abu Simbel
He meets Thomas Young in London to compare their two decipherment methods
He presents his method to the Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, in a letter to Bon-Joseph Dacier
quiz_supplementaire.explication: This is the day Champollion presents his method to the Academy, in the *Lettre à M. Dacier*, a text that would not appear in print until the end of October 1822.
